sections.h2: Who values and who bills property in Clark County, Ohio?
sections.html:
Two county offices split the job. The Clark County Auditor sets the value of every parcel, and the Clark County Treasurer mails the bills and collects the money. Both work out of the A.B. Graham Building at 31 North Limestone Street in Springfield. The auditor's printed number is 937-521-1860, and the treasurer's is 937-521-1832.

The treasurer's page says the office collects about $135 million a year in real estate taxes, plus $275,000 in manufactured home taxes. A bill combines levies from several local taxing bodies, so the rate depends on where the house sits.

The treasurer's property tax page offers a printed rate sheet for each tax year. Pick one up at the office or print it from the page when you want the levy breakdown for your district.

sections.h2: How often does Clark County reappraise homes?
sections.html:
Ohio law requires county auditors to reappraise every property once every six years and to run a triennial update in the third year of that cycle. The Clark County Auditor's triennial update FAQ says a reappraisal involves a visual inspection, while an update works only from sales in the three prior years. The 2022 update used sales from 2019, 2020 and 2021 and values as of January 1, 2022.

The FAQ describes a mass appraisal done by a hired contractor across more than 50,000 residential parcels. It lists location, lot size, age, style, square footage, construction quality, foundation, outbuildings and condition as the factors that feed a value. It also states how a value turns into a bill: appraised value times 35 percent times the voted levies gives the gross tax, and most rates are adjusted each year to raise the same revenue as the year before.

sections.h2: What are the Clark County payment dates and late charges?
sections.html:
Taxes are paid in two halves. For the 2025 tax year, the treasurer's page lists a first-half due date of February 27, 2026 and a second-half due date of August 7, 2026, and both dates have passed. Dates differ from cycle to cycle, so use the bill and the treasurer's page for each new cycle. Bills go out 20 to 25 days before the due date, and the page warns that a missing bill does not excuse the tax or the penalty.

A mailed payment counts as on time if the Postal Service postmark falls on or before the last day. Under section 323.12, a private meter postmark does not count.

sections.h2: Can you spread Clark County property tax into monthly payments?
sections.html:
Yes. The treasurer runs an escrow program that splits each semi-annual bill into monthly installments. You sign an escrow agreement, receive monthly coupons, and may pay more or less than the estimate each month. The page lists cash, check, money order or ACH debit as accepted methods and states there is no service charge.

  • Return the Escrow Program Form to the treasurer at P.O. Box 1305, Springfield, OH 45501-1305, or email treasurer@clarkcountyohio.gov.
  • Any balance left after your prepayments must be paid by the due date to avoid the late penalty.
  • Send address changes to the treasurer in writing so bills reach the right person.

Owners who are listing a house should ask the treasurer how any prepaid balance is applied at closing.

sections.h2: What is the route for contesting a Clark County valuation?
sections.html:
File a complaint with the county auditor on or before March 31 of the following year, or the closing date of first-half collection, whichever is later. That rule is in section 5715.19. A mailed complaint is timely if its postal postmark carries the deadline date, and a private meter mark does not qualify. Owners, spouses and certain retained professionals may file.

  • The auditor sends the complaint to the Clark County Board of Revision, which must rule within 180 days of the filing deadline.
  • The auditor's FAQ says you must bring evidence, and names a recent arm's length sale of your property or a comparable one as the best kind.
  • While a complaint is pending you may pay tax on your claimed value, and the treasurer shall accept it.
  • A taxpayer who files a complaint cannot file again in the same interim period unless something changed, such as a sale, casualty loss or major improvement.

Before filing, try the auditor's informal review, which the FAQ recommends first.

sections.h2: Which relief programs cut a Clark County tax bill?
sections.html:
Ohio's homestead exemption is the main one. The Department of Taxation explains that it shields part of a home's market value from tax for seniors 65 and older, permanently and totally disabled owners, and certain surviving spouses. For tax year 2026 the credit covers tax on up to $29,700 of value, and the income threshold is $41,000. Disabled veterans get a larger amount, $59,400, with no income test.

  • Apply with the Clark County Auditor on form DTE 105A, or DTE 105I for disabled veterans, by December 31 of the year you want the credit.
  • Age 65 must be reached by December 31 of the application year, and you must own and live in the house as of January 1.
  • If the auditor denies the application, file DTE 106B with the Board of Revision inside 60 days of receiving the denial.

House Bill 96 of 2025 lets county commissioners add a matching local-option exemption. Ask the auditor whether Clark County has adopted it.

sections.h2: What should a Clark County seller do about unpaid taxes?
sections.html:
Taxes follow the parcel, so any buyer or title company will find a balance. Ask the treasurer at 937-521-1832 for a payoff figure and give it to the closing agent, who can pay it from the sale proceeds. Penalties and interest on the schedule above keep building until the day it is paid, so an early payoff costs less than a late one.

The deed also carries a tax question. Under section 319.202, the buyer must confirm that the seller says no homestead or owner-occupancy reduction is hanging on the current or preceding year's taxes, or else attach a sworn estimate of the reduction. Know your own status before closing.

sections.h2: What does Clark County look like for homeowners?
sections.html:
Clark County covers 403 square miles of west central Ohio, with Springfield as its seat. Wikipedia lists Springfield and New Carlisle as its cities and reports that about a quarter of residents (25.4 percent) were rural in 2020. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts page adds:

  • Households: 55,975 for 2020 to 2024, at 2.37 people each.
  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $169,900, with monthly owner costs of $1,262 for those with a mortgage and $523 for those without.
  • Employer establishments: 2,196 in 2023, with total employment of 42,831.
  • Median household income: $63,132, and 14.1 percent of people in poverty.

faqs.q: What is the phone number for the Clark County Treasurer?
faqs.a: The treasurer's property tax page gives 937-521-1832 for questions about tax bills, and the county directory lists the office at 31 North Limestone Street in Springfield.

faqs.q: When was the second half of the 2025 Clark County tax due?
faqs.a: August 7, 2026. The first half was due February 27, 2026. Penalties of 5 percent and then 10 percent followed each date, as listed on the treasurer's page.

faqs.q: Where do I file a property value complaint in Clark County?
faqs.a: File it with the Clark County Auditor, who sends it to the Board of Revision. The deadline is March 31 of the following year or the close of first-half collection, whichever is later.

faqs.q: Does Clark County have a monthly tax payment plan?
faqs.a: Yes. The treasurer's escrow program divides each semi-annual bill into monthly payments with no service charge. Submit the Escrow Program Form to the treasurer at P.O. Box 1305, Springfield.

faqs.q: How does Clark County turn market value into a tax bill?
faqs.a: The auditor's FAQ says appraised value is multiplied by 35 percent and then by the voted levies to get the gross tax. Credits such as the homestead exemption are applied afterward.
